name: Larynx
func: The voice box at the top of the windpipe. It holds the vocal folds that make sound, and it guards the airway: it closes tight when you swallow and triggers a cough if anything goes down the wrong way.

levels.kid:
The **larynx** is your **voice box**. It sits in the front of your neck, at the top of your windpipe. The bump some people have in the front of the neck, the **Adam's apple**, is part of it.

Inside are two little stretchy flaps called **vocal folds** (people often say vocal cords). When you breathe quietly, they're open. When you talk or sing, they come together and the air you breathe out makes them buzz really fast. That buzz is your voice! Tight folds make high sounds and loose folds make low sounds.

The larynx is also a guard. When you swallow, it shuts and a little lid called the **epiglottis** folds over it, so food goes down the food pipe instead. If a crumb sneaks in, it makes you cough it out.
levels.hs:
The **larynx** lies in the front of the neck from about **C3 to C6** in adults, connecting the **pharynx** above to the **trachea** below. In front of it are the thin strap muscles; behind it is the **laryngopharynx**, which leads into the esophagus. The **thyroid gland** wraps around the trachea just below, and the **carotid sheaths** run on either side.

Its framework is made of cartilages joined by membranes and ligaments:
- **Thyroid cartilage**: the biggest, shaped like a shield; its front ridge is the **laryngeal prominence (Adam's apple)**.
- **Cricoid cartilage**: a complete ring, like a signet ring with the wide part at the back. It is the only complete cartilage ring in the airway.
- Two **arytenoid cartilages**: small pyramids sitting on the back of the cricoid; the vocal folds attach to them.
- **Epiglottis**: a leaf-shaped elastic cartilage that folds back over the entrance during swallowing.

Muscles move the arytenoids to **open (abduct)** the vocal folds for breathing, **close (adduct)** them for speech and swallowing, and **tense** them to change pitch.

The larynx has three jobs: **protecting the airway**, **phonation** (making sound), and helping you build up chest pressure for coughing and straining by closing tight.
levels.college:
The laryngeal cavity has three regions: the **supraglottis** (above the vocal folds, including the **vestibular or "false" folds**), the **glottis** (the true vocal folds and the gap between them, the **rima glottidis**), and the **subglottis** (down to the lower edge of the cricoid).

**Intrinsic muscles**:
- **Posterior cricoarytenoid**: the **only abductor**, opening the airway. Losing it on both sides is dangerous.
- **Lateral cricoarytenoid**, **transverse and oblique arytenoids**: adductors.
- **Thyroarytenoid** (its inner part is the **vocalis**): shortens and relaxes the folds and fine-tunes them.
- **Cricothyroid**: tilts the thyroid cartilage forward on the cricoid, **lengthening and tensing** the folds to raise pitch.

**Nerves** (both from the vagus):
- **Superior laryngeal nerve**: its **internal branch** gives sensation above the vocal folds (the trigger for the cough reflex); its **external branch** supplies the cricothyroid.
- **Recurrent laryngeal nerve**: supplies **all other intrinsic muscles** and sensation below the folds. On the left it loops under the **aortic arch**; on the right under the **subclavian artery**. Both then climb in the tracheoesophageal grooves, entering the larynx behind the cricothyroid joint, close to the thyroid gland's inferior thyroid artery.

**Blood supply** comes from the superior and inferior laryngeal arteries (branches of the superior and inferior thyroid arteries).

During swallowing the larynx is pulled **up and forward** by the suprahyoid muscles, the epiglottis tips back, and the vocal and vestibular folds close: three layers of protection.

Lymphatics are sparse at the glottis, which matters for cancer spread.
levels.phd:
Sound is produced according to the **myoelastic–aerodynamic theory**. Subglottic pressure pushes the adducted folds apart; the elastic recoil of the tissue and the **Bernoulli effect** (pressure dropping in the fast airflow between the folds) pull them back together. Because the lower edges open before the upper edges, energy is transferred to the folds each cycle and they keep oscillating, typically at about 100–250 Hz in conversation.

The **body–cover model** explains why the folds vibrate so well. The vocal fold has a layered structure: squamous epithelium; **Reinke's space** (the superficial lamina propria, loose and gel-like); the intermediate and deep lamina propria forming the **vocal ligament**; and the **vocalis** muscle. The loose cover rides over the stiffer body as a **mucosal wave**, visible with **stroboscopy**. Scarring of Reinke's space stiffens the cover and degrades the voice.

Pitch rises with tension (cricothyroid) and falls as the vocalis thickens the folds. Loudness depends mainly on subglottic pressure. The **vocal tract** (pharynx, mouth, nose) filters the buzz into vowels; this is the **source–filter theory** of speech.

**Brainstem control**: motor neurons for the intrinsic muscles sit in the **nucleus ambiguus** in the medulla. Laryngeal sensory fibres reach the **nucleus tractus solitarius**. The **laryngeal adductor reflex** closes the glottis within about 20–30 milliseconds of stimulation. Voluntary speech involves the **laryngeal motor cortex**, a region in humans with an unusually direct projection to brainstem motor neurons, thought to be one ingredient of our vocal-learning ability.

Developmentally, the laryngeal cartilages derive from the **4th and 6th pharyngeal arches**, which explains the vagal branches: superior laryngeal nerve (arch 4) and recurrent laryngeal nerve (arch 6). The recurrent nerve's loop around arch arteries explains its long course.
levels.expert:
**Hoarseness** lasting over 3 weeks warrants a look at the larynx, by **flexible nasendoscopy** or **laryngoscopy**, with stroboscopy for vibration.

**Vocal fold palsy**:
- **Unilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve** injury: hoarse, breathy voice and weak cough; the fold sits near the midline (paramedian).
- **Bilateral** injury: both folds sit near the midline, so the voice may be fair but there is **stridor** and the airway is at risk, sometimes needing a tracheostomy.
- Causes: **thyroid surgery**, **anterior cervical spine surgery**, carotid surgery, and on the left, lung cancer or aortic arch aneurysm pressing on the nerve near the arch (called Ortner or cardiovocal syndrome when the cause is cardiovascular).

**Neuro relevance**: a **lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome** damages the nucleus ambiguus, causing hoarseness and **dysphagia**. Vagus nerve schwannomas and skull-base tumours at the **jugular foramen** cause vocal fold palsy with other lower cranial nerve deficits. Neurodegenerative disease (e.g. motor neuron disease, Parkinson disease) causes weak, slurred or quiet voice and aspiration risk; **spasmodic dysphonia** is a focal laryngeal dystonia.

**Other lesions**: **vocal nodules** (paired, at the junction of front and middle thirds, from voice overuse), **polyps**, **Reinke's oedema** (in long-term smokers), and **laryngeal cancer** (mostly squamous cell, linked to smoking). Glottic cancers cause early hoarseness and spread late (few lymphatics), so they're often caught early; supraglottic cancers spread to neck nodes earlier.

**Emergencies**: **epiglottitis** (drooling, tripod posture, "thumb sign" on lateral neck X-ray) and **croup** (barking cough, "steeple sign" of subglottic narrowing on frontal X-ray) in children. In an airway emergency the **cricothyroid membrane** is the surgical access point.

keyPoints: Voice box from C3–C6, between pharynx and trachea
Cartilages: thyroid, cricoid (complete ring), arytenoids, epiglottis
Posterior cricoarytenoid is the only abductor
Recurrent laryngeal nerve supplies all intrinsic muscles except cricothyroid
Left recurrent nerve loops under the aortic arch

test.q: The only muscle that opens (abducts) the vocal folds is the ______.
test.explain: Losing both posterior cricoarytenoids leaves the folds closed, threatening the airway.

test.q: Which nerve supplies the cricothyroid muscle?
test.explain: The external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve supplies cricothyroid; injury lowers voice range and pitch control.

test.q: Which cartilage forms a complete ring?
test.explain: The cricoid is the only complete cartilage ring in the airway.

test.q: After thyroid surgery a patient is hoarse with a breathy voice. Most likely injured nerve?
test.explain: The recurrent laryngeal nerve runs in the tracheoesophageal groove right next to the thyroid.

test.q: The motor nucleus in the medulla for the laryngeal muscles is the nucleus ______.
test.explain: The nucleus ambiguus supplies the muscles of the pharynx and larynx through cranial nerves IX and X.
